big: Rohan's SIP bounced twice. He has no idea why, and he is afraid it will be cancelled. The answer sits in two dates on the calendar.

lines: My SIP failed twice this year. Is it cancelled? I have money in my account most of the month.
Most of the month is not the same as on the day. Let us follow the money across the month, twice.

alt: A month strip showing salary on the 7th and an SIP on the 5th, then moved to the 10th
caps: Rohan's salary arrives on the 7th. His SIP is set for the 5th.
On the 5th the account holds only ₹2,000. The instalment bounces, and the bank may charge a fee.
Now the SIP date moves to the 10th, three days after payday.
The money is there, so the instalment is paid.

q: Rohan's salary credits on the 7th and his SIP debits on the 5th. What is the best fix?
opts: Move the SIP date to a few days after salary arrives
Change to a different fund house
Keep the date and top up the account on the 4th each month
Stop the SIP and invest a lump sum each year
why: A debit date shortly after payday matches money to the mandate, and it is a one-time change.
The fund house is not the problem. The date falls before the money arrives, whichever house it is.
Topping up on the 4th works only if he remembers every month. One slip and it bounces again.
A yearly lump sum gives up the habit and the averaging that made the SIP worth doing.

q: Rohan's SIP has bounced twice. He is told 'a third miss in a row may cancel it'. What should he do?
opts: Wait to see whether a third instalment also fails before doing anything
Change the date, keep a buffer, and check the mandate is still active
Cancel the SIP himself so that the record on his folio stays clean
Start a second SIP in another fund to make up for the missed ones
why: Waiting risks the third miss and the loss of the SIP. The fix is available now.
Moving the date and keeping a cushion fix the cause, and checking the mandate shows nothing has already lapsed.
Cancelling ends the habit he wants to keep. Bounces are about timing, not about the SIP being a bad idea.
A second SIP adds a second mandate to bounce, and fixes nothing about the date.

q: When is a 'pause' or 'skip' option on an SIP a fair use?
opts: When the market falls sharply and he feels nervous about his units
For a genuine cash need, such as a medical bill, with a plan to restart
Whenever he sees an advertisement for a better fund than his own
Whenever the NAV has gone up compared with the month before
why: A fall is when the same instalment buys more units. Pausing out of nerves means skipping the cheap months.
A real cash need is what the option is for, and a restart date keeps the habit.
Chasing a new fund each month adds cost and timing guesses, and the SIP loses its steady habit.
A higher NAV means fewer units this month, not a reason to stop. Over time, high and low months even out.

q: Why does an emergency fund protect an SIP?
opts: It pays the fund's own expense ratio each year on his behalf
So a sudden bill does not force him to stop or sell equity in a hurry
It raises the return the SIP earns on every instalment he makes
It cancels the mandate automatically whenever a crisis arrives
why: The expense ratio is deducted from the fund itself, so an emergency fund has no role in paying it at all.
With six months of cash set aside, a bill never touches the SIP or forces a sale at a bad price.
An emergency fund earns a small return of its own. It does not change what the SIP earns.
A mandate stays active until he cancels it, or repeated misses end it. A cash buffer helps avoid those misses.

pts: Set the SIP date a few days after payday.
Keep a buffer in the account, so an instalment never bounces.
Pause for real cash needs, not for market fear, and keep an emergency fund.
